explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, is told, “write down today’s date.” I would have checked the calendar three times and still written it in pencil, just to be safe. God gives the reason right away: on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem.

A list of names sounds so official, friend. I can almost see the clipboard. But God never asks Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, for any names. He says, “write down today’s date,” and that's the whole job.

I'd love a song here too, friend, but this isn't that kind of morning. Ezekiel, a priest living among the exiles, gets no tune and no lyrics. God tells him, “write down today’s date,” and then tells him what is happening on that very day.
Jerusalem it is, baker. God says that on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to it. That's why the date matters. Ezekiel is told to write it down so the day gets a place on the record.

Nineveh is a real city in the Bible, friend, but it's not the one here. God says the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem, and that's the city named in the text. I think it's an easy mix-up, since city names can run together like cookie dough left too long in the bowl.

Damascus is a real city in the Bible too, baker, but it isn't named here. God tells Ezekiel that on this very day the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem. The date goes down on paper, and Jerusalem is the city it belongs to.

True, baker. God says, “Take the choicest of the flock and pile the fuel beneath it. Bring it to a boil and cook the bones in it.” The fuel goes under the pot first, and then comes the boil. Nobody is rushing this recipe, and I've never been so glad my ovens come with a timer.
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. God says to pile the fuel beneath the pot and bring it to a boil, and then to cook the bones in it. Both steps are right there in Ezekiel 24:5.

The king of Babylon is in this passage, friend, but he's not in the woe. He shows up back in verse 2 as the one who has laid siege to Jerusalem. The woe goes to “the city of bloodshed” and “the pot now rusted.” God puts those two side by side, so the rusted pot isn't the king.

That's right, baker. The king of Babylon appears earlier, laying siege to Jerusalem. In the woe, God says, “Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted, whose rust will not come off!” The pot is paired with the city, not with the king.

On the bare rock, baker. God says, “she poured it out on the bare rock; she did not pour it on the ground to cover it with dust.” Bare rock has nothing to cover it. That's a heavy picture, and I think it's meant to be.

The Jordan is a famous river, friend, but it isn't in this verse. God says the blood was poured out “on the bare rock.” He also says it wasn't poured on the ground to cover it with dust. This is a heavy part, so I'll stay close to what the text says.

A city gate feels like a natural spot, friend, but the text never says it. God says the city “poured it out on the bare rock.” The verse also says she didn't pour it on the ground to cover it with dust. This is one of the heavy parts, so I'll keep it simple.

explanations.answer: To stir up wrath and take vengeance
explanations.explanation: That's what God says, baker. His words are, “In order to stir up wrath and take vengeance, I have placed her blood on the bare rock, so that it would not be covered.” This is a heavy verse, friend. I'm not going to add anything to what He says.

explanations.answer: To warn the nations all around
explanations.explanation: Warning the nations sounds like a reasonable purpose, friend, but the text doesn't say it. God gives His own reason: “to stir up wrath and take vengeance.” The nations aren't mentioned in these verses at all. I'll leave it where the text leaves it.

explanations.answer: To call the priests to pray
explanations.explanation: Priests and prayer are in the Bible plenty, baker, but not in this verse. God gives the reason Himself. He says He placed her blood on the bare rock “to stir up wrath and take vengeance.” That's the reason the text gives.
Burned is the word, baker. God says, “let the bones be burned.” Back in verse 5 those same bones were part of the choicest of the flock. Now the fire is piled high, and the bones are in it.
Buried is a good guess, friend, but that isn't the word here. This pot is on a pile of logs with the fire kindled. God says, “let the bones be burned.” Nothing in the verse says to bury anything.

I know that would be a happier ending, baker, but that's not what the verse says. God tells them to pile on the logs and kindle the fire, then says, “let the bones be burned.” Saved isn't in the verse. This is a hard picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: Melt its impurity and burn off its rust
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, “Then its impurity will melt within; its rust will be consumed.” The empty pot sits on the coals until it's hot and its copper glows. I've scrubbed a baking sheet or two in my day, and I never once had this kind of heat to help.

explanations.answer: Make it shine bright for a feast
explanations.explanation: A shiny pot for a feast would be a lovely picture, friend, but it's not in this verse. God says the heat will melt the impurity within and consume the rust. Nothing here says it's for a feast. The glow is the copper getting hot on the coals.

explanations.answer: Harden it so it never cracks
explanations.explanation: That's a clever guess, baker, but the verse says something different. God says the pot sits on its coals “until it becomes hot and its copper glows.” Then its impurity will melt within, and its rust will be consumed. Hardening isn't mentioned at all.

The text says the opposite, friend. God says, “It has frustrated every effort; its thick rust has not been removed, even by the fire.” The rust is still there. Even that blazing heat didn't get it off.

That's right, baker. God says the pot “has frustrated every effort” and that its thick rust “has not been removed, even by the fire.” The rust is stuck on. I've met a few stubborn stains in my time, but nothing like this.

Cleanse is the word, baker. God says, “I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness.” The pot talk has stopped, and now He's speaking straight to “you.” It's a heavy line, and it's said plainly.

Warn is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. God says, “I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness.” The word is cleanse, and it matches the pot with its rust that wouldn't come off.

Test doesn't show up in this verse, baker. God says, “I tried to cleanse you, but you would not be purified from your filthiness.” That ties back to the rust that wouldn't come off. The word God uses is cleanse.
That's it, baker. God says, “You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided.” The verse gives that one condition. This is a serious line, and it's good to let it be serious.

explanations.answer: Until the king of Babylon leaves
explanations.explanation: The king of Babylon does appear in this passage, friend, back in verse 2, laying siege to Jerusalem. But God doesn't tie being pure again to him leaving. He says, “You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided.”

explanations.answer: Until you bring a new offering
explanations.explanation: An offering is a reasonable thing to think of, baker, but it isn't in this verse. God says, “You will not be pure again until My wrath against you has subsided.” Nothing is said here about bringing anything.

True, baker. God says, “I will not refrain or show pity, nor will I relent.” It's said plainly, and it follows right after “the time is coming, and I will act.” This is a heavy line, so I'll let it stand.
The text says it the other way, friend. God says, “I will not refrain or show pity, nor will I relent.” That's what He says in verse 14. It's a heavy line, and I'm not going to soften it.

Right, baker. God says, “I will judge you according to your ways and deeds,” and then adds, “declares the Lord GOD.” That's how He closes the parable. It's a heavy ending, and I'll leave it as He said it.
Prophets are all over the Bible, friend, but they aren't named in this closing line. God says, “I will judge you according to your ways and deeds.” That's the standard He gives here.

Kings do come up in this passage, baker, since the king of Babylon laid siege to Jerusalem back in verse 2. But the closing line doesn't say a thing about promises. God says, “I will judge you according to your ways and deeds.”
